body: Fort Fredrick, also known as Trincomalee Fort or Fort of Triquillimale, is a historically rich landmark in Trincomalee, Eastern Province, Sri Lanka. Constructed by the Portuguese in 1624 CE, the fort was built on the picturesque Swami Rock-Konamamalai using debris from the ancient and renowned Hindu Koneswaram temple, also known as the Temple of a Thousand Pillars. The destruction of this temple by the Portuguese colonial Constantino de Sá de Noronha under Phillip III marked a significant historical event, and remnants of this past are intertwined with the fort's construction.Inside the fort, a new village was established, inhabited by Portuguese and Tamil people, alongside 50 Portuguese soldiers. A church named Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe was also built, adding to the cultural and religious tapestry of the area. In 1665, the Dutch dismantled and rebuilt the fort, renaming it Fort Fredrick.Visitors today can enjoy the breathtaking views surrounding the fort, making it a must-visit destination in Trincomalee. The ticket prices are quite reasonable, costing Rs. 120.00 for locals and $6.50 for foreigners, with tickets available until 6 pm. Fort Fredrick is not only a place of historical significance but also a site of incredible natural beauty, offering an enriching experience for all who visit.
title: Fort Fredrick, also known as Trincomalee Fort or Fort of Triquillimale

body: I was really interested to see this fort, as it was occupied by the British for a long time, though it was originally built in 16-something by the Portuguese. It's still a military base for the Sri Lankan army, but you can enter through the ancient archway and walk right up to the top of the hill, so you pass all the military buildings that the British left, which are still in use. As well as barracks etc., there is a large mansion called Wellesley House, where the Duke of Wellington stayed. Unfortunately it's not open to the public. The upper part is not military, and the road passes rows of shops selling gifts and items related to the temple at the very top. The first thing you see as you approach is a huge statue of a Hindu god (not sure which), surrounded by enormous cows and people. There are several different shrines on the edge of the cliffs, some of which have ancient images saved or rediscovered from the original temple, before the Portuguese destroyed it. The temple itself is fairly modern and very colourful both outside and in, with statues, images and paintings which tell the story of the original temple and its destruction. The views from the rock are impressive, you can see far up and down the coast, and over the town and harbour. There are crowds of spotted deer roaming around the fort and the temple, which are delightful to watch, particularly for children. On my way down, I stopped at a little cafe with an amazing view, for a drink and a chat with other visitors. Altogether a very interesting experience, which I'll never forget.
title: Historic fort and impressive Hindu temple.

body: Trincomalee also known as Gokanna, is the administrative headquarters of the Trincomalee District and major resort port city of Eastern Province, Sri Lanka. Located on the east coast of the island overlooking the Trincomalee Harbour, 113 miles south of Jaffna and 69 miles north of Batticaloa, Trincomalee has been one of the main centres of Sri Lankan Tamil language speaking culture on the island for over two millennia. With a population of 99,135, the city is built on a peninsula of the same name, which divides its inner and outer harbours. People from Trincomalee are known as Trincomalians and the local authority is Trincomalee Urban Council. Trincomalee city is home to the famous Koneswaram temple alluded to in its historic Tamil name Thirukonamalai and is home to other historical monuments such as the Bhadrakali Amman Temple, Trincomalee, the Trincomalee Hindu Cultural Hall and, opened in 1897, the Trincomalee Hindu College. Trincomalee is also the site of the Trincomalee railway station and an ancient ferry service to Jaffna and the south side of the harbour at Muttur.
title: Tincomalee '' feel the Sea Wind''

body: So far we've visited a few old Dutch forts in our trip around SL. Fort Frederick has been the best so far. (Jaffna Fort is pretty much destroyed and Galle Fort is mostly lots of modern shops and advertising signs) Fort Frederick is amazing. Its like as if the Dutch have just left and it's all been preserved. It's used today by the army so you can't access any building - only admire them as you walk or drive along the road. The buildings are so old and yet appeared cared for and well maintained. There were lots of deer wandering around which added to the serenity. We got a tuk tuk through the Fort to the temple at the top of the hill. We checked out the temple and then walks back down through the Fort - 15 min walk at the mostA tip - walk down - don't try walking up the hill
title: Best Fort in Sri Lanka

body: This fort wall is infact the entrance to Koneswaram Temple and inside we get to see the Military effect. The fort is exactly bordering the sea. body: It would be good to walk to the top of the Fort as it gives you the opportunity to see the Fort. Lot of places to click some good pictures. Since there is an Army Camp on the Fort, you will see a lot of personnel. The highlight is the Deer, can be seen everywhere around the Fort.

body: Well worth a few hours walk . You start by passing a large stupa with an interesting large hole in the "bulb" bit high up . As it is infront of an army barracks a gun emplacement springs to mind . It's a pleasant shaded walk up through the barracks with many deer in evidence . You pop out at the top and pass by many stalls selling the usual temple tat with a rather colorful shivite temple which also offers a wonderful view of the bay . you will have to deposit your shoes at the top so prepare for burnt feet also there is a very nice juice bar just before you enter the temple which is worthy of a stop .
title: Interesting walk

body: The big must see in Trincomalee. Fort Frederick was originallybuilt by the Portugese in 1623 and captured by the Dutch in1782. British from 1796 until Ceylon's independence. It is nowa very attractive mix of modern military base, massive ancienttrees, Hindu temple, wild life, colonial history and sea views.Colonial buildings include Wellesley Lodge named after theDuke of Wellington who stayed there in 1800. The templeis Koneswaram Kovil is one of the five holiest Shaive templesin Sri Lanka. Wild life includes free roaming deer. Sea views might include whales which pass along this coast.Strongly recommended if you are visiting the East Coast ofSri Lanka.
title: Attractive must see in Trincomalee

body: Witnessed this ancient fort which was governed by three different foreign nationalities of the past started in the early 17th century. This has become an army camp and access is limited to see the whole area, unless if there is a known officer to take you around. Still you see the entrance and little bit of inside old buildings. Not well maintained like the Galle fort but worth seeing if you are in Trinco. You can see lots of deer freely roaming around. Don't forget don't feed them.
title: On the way to the Temple

body: The former Dutch and British colonial fort occupies the base of the peninsula and is now a military zone that you pass through on the way to Koneswaram Temple. There are indeed many deer around.
title: Former Dutch Fort

body: Great sea views presumably in the pasr for defence en route to the Koneswaram Temple. Through a huge gate and onto the site. Many old buildings in part a bit like a museum. Kept in good condition
title: Great location

body: I found Fort Frederick quite interesting and worth visiting. It is an operational Sri Lankan military base so access to many parts is restricted but there is still much of the original fort to see as well as other parts of the base. There is also a significant kovil to see.There are also great areas where you can watch the local Trinco fishing fleets heading out. (or in)
title: Historically significant.

body: You have to enter the fort to reach the kovil at the top of the hill. There's not much to see inside the fort itself. There are some very old trees, a Buddhist temple (be aware that a young monk at this temple will ask you to pay 200 rupees per person as entrance fee). The old fort gate is beautiful as are the walls viewed from the outside of the fort.
title: Not much to see

body: Fort Frederick is worth visiting and it definitely worth researching the long and complex history of it before you go. It is a fort area constructed by the Portuguese and Dutch and completed in 1624, situated high on Swarmi Rock. Only certain parts of it are open to the public and it has not been developed in the same way as Galle Fort. It is worth entering through the narrow granite gate to walk to the top of the rock to see the spectacular Hindu temple and magnificent views. On the way you will see beautiful deer and very likely peacocks which wander freely.
title: Of great historic significance

body: This is an impressive structure with a long and colourful history. Sadly, the SL military have fenced off most of it for their own use. Public access is severely restriced to a walk through the grounds along a tarmac road between two fences all the way to the temple at the top. If you're not interested in the temple you may aswell stop at the fort gates and save yourself a hot climb.
title: Restricted Access

body: The Old Dutch Fort wall or fortress is sadly in a dilapidated state as the government of Sri Lanka has not bothered to repair or maintain it. There is only a partial wall that is to be seen from the road. There is however, a gateway that was the original entrance to the fort still active and one can drive through this gateway, which is quite quaint. Once you drive through the gateway, you enter the Old Dutch Fort itself and this is now being used as a Sri Lankan Military Base. You can still see the trees that were planted by the Dutch in the yards of the Military Base, which really are quite amazing. You can also see the old buildings that are used by the military, but sadly they are not being maintained as well as they should be.If you happen to be travelling to Trincomalee, then I suggest a drive through the gateway and through the roads to see the Trincomalee Dutch Fort.
title: Not looked after, but worth a visit

body: this is enroute the Kineswaram temple. currently used by military and protected site.. Dears and peacoks are roming around and place is well maintained . the beach beside the fort is also good and a good picture spot..

body: Originally constructed by the Portuguese and then reconstructed by the Dutch in 1675 the Fort fell to the British later, who probably gave it its present name. Most of the area is occupied by the armed forces and the police, and the Fort is inevitably visited by pilgrims and foreigners alike because the famous Koneswaran Temple is located inside. A herd of spotted deer freely roam inside the premises.
title: Must visit if in Trincomalee

body: Nice place to walk and see the cliff. At the end there is a temple. Through the way you can see many cute animals :) best to see if the weather is not the best for the beach

There are toilets half way up the hill but you must pay and provide own paper.As we were leaving a monk insisted that we pay a fee. This was not an entry fee just a fee for him being there – a bit rude I thought !
title: Ok - watch out for the onsite monk!

body: As with most tourist places in Sri Lanka, there is a lack of written history on plaques, boards, etc. A tourist will have to google the place to read about it's history. It does not clearly show which parts were built by the Portuguese, the Dutch or the Brits. But we did manage to explore the area ourselves and hope that the SL military who occupy parts of the fort will contribute to its preservation. Overall a place to visit if you get the right commentary from a vocal who know something of its history.
title: Lack of written history

body: This is an old deutche fort that stands as a symbol of the history and still in use. Inside, on top of the mountain rock is the most famous hindu temple, Koneshwaram, which was rebuilt later. There is a security forces base inside the fort as well as some of the government departments. Deers can be seen around. Please don't throw polythene bags away as the deers eat them and die. When you climb to the top, to the temple you can have an amazing view of the Indian ocean. The sea is very deep beyond the rock and it is thrilling to see the dark deep waters from that height. If you are in Trincomalee, must visit here.

body: Ideal time to visit is either in the morning around 8 a.m. or around 4 p.m. when it is cool and shady. Be prepared to spend about one hour. If you are adventurous, walk it from the ground level from the Trinco town Dutch bay. The Dutch bay itself is a beauty with absolute turquoise coloured sea water and a fantastic beach to dip into, during the season April to August.There is a small climb to Fort Frederick. The entrance portal is very interesting and similar in construction to the portals of the Galle Fort and Matara Fort. The garden and environs are relaxing if, one takes the time to absorb the view overlooking the bay and climb up to the ancient garrison Fort. It also houses the Koneshwaram Kovil. Do not miss this visit.

body: This is the entrance to Koneswaram Temple. The history goes back to Ramayana, Ravana had worshiped and patronized this temple. That temple had lots of structures when the Portuguese and Dutch invaded then Ceylon they removed the stone structures and built this Gate and Fort. It is still in Majestic appearance. This is presently occupied by Military, there is no much of restrictions but be cautious of taking photographs. There are lots of Deer in this area. There is no Entry fee. worth making a trip. If you are going to Koneswaram temple you will be going through this gate and area.
title: Prehistory monument

body: Fort Fredrick or Fort of Triquillimale as known by the Portuguese, was built by them on Swami Rock-Konamamalai from the debris of the world famous ancient and prehistoric Hindu Koneswaram temple (The temple of a thousand pillars), which is said to be the original temple of Koneswaram built by the archetypal Lord of Lanka, King Ravana. The original kovil was destroyed on April 14, 1622 CE, the Tamil New Years Day, by the Portuguese general Constantino de Sá de Noronha. The great pillars and building blocks of the kovil itself was recycled in the building of the fort. Its treasures were philandered by de Sa de Noronha, who was famous for his greed for treasure. Little of this fortune is said to have reached the treasury of Portugal. The fort was later occupied by the Dutch, and last the British. Today it houses some detachments of the Sri Lanka military. Worth a visit and a walk or bike ride.

Stopped to see the deer on the way back from Koneswaram Temple
body: Our child liked seeing the deer. We enjoyed the green grass and sea breeze and saw some recruits in infantry training drilling on the field. It's worth a stop if you are visiting the must see Koneswaram Temple.

title: Interesting walls and surrounds
body: This appears to still be a working barracks but entry through the fort gates and along the road leading to temple is unrestricted. Impressive thick stone walls as approach, historic guns outside and impressively deep entrance portico. Once inside, many buildings but none of which appear open to public or provide additional information and as a result there is nothing of much interest. There are toilets half way up the hill but you must pay and provide own paper.

title: A nice stroll.
body: We walked through the fort on the main road three times while we were in Trinco. It was a nice cool early morning or evening stroll and the buildings within the walls are quite interesting even though as it is a military post, you can only see them from the road. The tame deer that roam the site are everywhere and when you get to the top of the hill, it's worth it to remove your shoes, to have a look at the Hindu Kovil and the view down to the sea below from there.

title: well maintained
body: The row of boutiques near the kovil which covers the view of the Harbour should be removed by the Govt.

title: The Stomping Ground of Colonel Wellesley
body: The Temple of a Thousand Pillars was destroyed by the Portuguese in the early part of the seventeenth century where upon they established the Fort of Triquillimalea, a key strategic position overlooking the Bay of Triquillimalea (later Dutch Bay or Baay Van Trincoenmale) and the Eastern Province coast up to Uppuveli and beyond to Nilaveli. The Dutch subsequently conquered the position and rebuilt the fortification and renamed it Fort Fredrick in 1665. There was much disquiet between the Dutch, French and German interests relating to the fortification until peace, law and order was established in 1795 and the Capture of Trincomalee by the British until Ceylon independence in 1948. Colonel Arthur Wellesley, later the 1st Duke of Wellington was stationed at Fort Frederick in 1800. He lived in Wellesley Lodge which has a long veranda where Colonel Wellesley was able to view Dutch Bay and two gun positions. In the ground floor there is a tethering chain which is still secured into the wall, where Colonel Wellesley tied his horse before it was taken back to the stables. Wellesley Lodge is out of bounds to the general public, but may be seen from the public road that leads to the Koneswaram Temple, it is now the Officers' Mess. Inside Fort Frederick you are able to see the garrison buildings being well looked after by the resident 2nd (Volunteer) battalion of the Gajaba Regiment, Sri Lankan Army. There is an Army Welfare Cafe that is very much like a British NAFFI where you can buy food, drink and military odds and sods on the public road.
